What Are Derivatives? Forwards, Futures, Options and Swaps

A derivative is a contract whose value depends on something else, such as a share, an index, a commodity or a currency. This guide compares the four main types and explains why they exist.

2 min readFor MBA, BBA and BBMUpdated 2 November 2026

An everyday example

A wheat farmer worries that prices may fall before harvest, and a flour mill worries they may rise. They agree today to trade 100 quintals in three months at ₹2,500 a quintal. That agreement is a derivative: it has value only because wheat has a price. Both sides have removed their price risk.

The four types compared

TypeWhat it isObligationWhere traded
ForwardA private agreement to trade at a set price on a future dateBoth sidesOver the counter
FuturesA standardised forwardBoth sidesExchange
OptionsThe right, not the obligation, to buy or sell at a set priceOnly the sellerExchange or over the counter
SwapAn exchange of cash flows over timeBoth sidesMostly over the counter

What derivatives are used for

  • Hedging: reducing an existing risk, such as an exporter locking in the dollar rate.
  • Speculation: taking a view on price with a small upfront margin, which brings high risk.
  • Arbitrage: profiting from a price gap between the spot and futures markets, which helps keep prices in line.

Exchange-traded and over-the-counter

BasisExchange-tradedOver the counter (OTC)
TermsStandardisedCustomised
Counterparty riskVery low, as the clearing corporation guarantees tradesHigher
TransparencyPrices are publicLimited
Regulation in IndiaSEBIMainly the RBI, for interest rate and currency contracts

Key terms

  • Underlying asset: what the contract is based on.
  • Lot size: the fixed contract quantity.
  • Expiry: the last day of the contract.
  • Margin: the deposit needed to hold a position.
  • Mark to market: daily settlement of gains and losses.
  • Open interest: the number of contracts still open.

The risks

Derivatives use leverage, so a small price move causes a large gain or loss relative to the money put up. SEBI studies have found that the great majority of individual traders in equity derivatives make losses, so students should learn the concepts first and practise without real money. Our paper trading tool lets you do this.

Exam and interview questions

What is the difference between forwards and futures?

Forwards are private, customised and carry counterparty risk. Futures are standardised, exchange-traded, marked to market daily and guaranteed by a clearing corporation.

What are the main participants in the derivatives market?

Hedgers, speculators and arbitrageurs. Hedgers reduce risk, speculators take it on, and arbitrageurs keep prices in line across markets.

What is an underlying asset?

The asset from which a derivative gets its value, such as a share, an index, a commodity, an interest rate or a currency.
